Which resume tool should I use?

It depends on what you’re missing. If you don’t have a resume, or you want the page designed for you, you need a builder: Kickresume, Rezi, Enhancv, and Teal all do that, free with limits and by subscription for the rest. If you have a resume and you’re tailoring it to many postings, you need a keyword scanner: Jobscan, or the matching inside Teal and Rezi. If you want it written for you, TopResume. The report’s limits, so you can weigh it fairly: it reads the words we pull from your file, not the design, and it is AI applying a recruiter’s criteria, not a person reading your resume. It gives no keyword score and no interview odds, and it won’t build, design, or track anything. How to negotiate a job offer
How to handle the salary question, the offer call, your number, the counter, and the close, with the research behind each step.
After the offer
Offer negotiation
Offer negotiation · a twelve-minute guide
Most offers have some room. Here's how to find it.

Our take, from the recruiter's side of the table: there's usually some room, and recruiters expect a good candidate to ask. Most people don't. The skill is asking in a way the recruiter can take to whoever approves the offer.
Offer includes equity? Read the tech guide
By the offer, everyone wants this to close

The company has spent weeks finding you and has often passed on other candidates to get here. The recruiter is measured on filling the seat. The hiring manager wants the work started. In our experience, a reasonable, specific ask gives them something to say yes to. It isn't risk-free: some offers are firm, and how you ask matters.

Plenty of people never ask. In a field experiment with real job ads, 9.4% of applicants negotiated pay when the ad didn't mention it, and 23.1% when the ad said pay was negotiable. In a 2025 experiment with US tech job seekers, 54% negotiated on their own, and a short note encouraging them raised that to 61%. The share who got better pay rose from 30% to 36%. In an older study of MBA graduates from one school, men who bargained ended up about 4% higher and women about 3%.
Our take:
even when the first answer is that the number is fixed, the room is often somewhere else: base, sign-on, equity, level, or start date. Your job is to find which one.
Before the offer, let them name the range

Early in the process you'll be asked what you're looking for. Answering with a number before you know the level and scope usually caps you. Ask for the range first. Many states and cities now require employers to share one.
They ask what you're looking for
The recruiter screen
I'd like to learn more about the scope and level before I put a number on it. Could you share the range you have for this role?
You have expectations, and you want the role defined before you price it. In our experience, most recruiters will share the range when asked directly.
They insist on a number
Give a range you'd be glad to hit
Based on what I know so far and what similar roles pay, I'm thinking somewhere in the range of [your target] to [a bit higher]. I'd want to revisit once we've talked about the level.

A researched range whose bottom is a number you'd be happy with. Never put your walk-away number at the bottom. In experiments, a range that started at the asker's target and reached higher won better terms than the target alone, without making the other side like them less.
They ask what you make now
Price the new role
I'd rather focus on what this role is worth. What range has the team set for it?
A redirect to the job in front of you. Many US states and cities restrict salary-history questions, and the rules differ by location, so check yours.
What the salary-history studies found
On the offer call, thank them and ask questions

When the recruiter calls with numbers, this isn't the negotiation yet. It's the fact-finding. Be warm about the role, hold back on reacting to the number, and leave with everything you need to decide.
Thank you, I'm really excited about this team. I'd like a couple of days to look at the whole package. Could I ask a few questions so I have the full picture?
What level is this, and what separates it from the next level up?
What's the range for this level in my location?
How is the bonus set, and what has it paid out in practice?
For equity: what type, how much, how it vests, and what the stated value is based on.
Is there a sign-on bonus, and does it have to be repaid if I leave early?
When do you need an answer, and can I have the offer in writing?
Pick your number
Before you counter, decide the one total you'd sign at. Everything else in the conversation is about how to get there.
Make the ask
The recruiter usually can't approve the change. They take it to a manager or a compensation team. Give them three things to carry: what you want, why, and what happens if they get there.

Ask on a call if you can. Start with genuine enthusiasm, name the number once, and keep it collaborative: you're working the problem together. How you ask matters. In experiments, evaluators were less willing to work with candidates who asked for more, and the penalty was usually larger for women.
Our advice:
tie a specific number to the role and treat the gap as a shared problem. It's the easiest kind of request for a recruiter to champion.
The offer is below your number
The counter
I'm excited about this and I want to make it work. Given the scope we discussed and the range for the level, I was looking for a total closer to [$X]. If we can get there, I'm ready to sign.
The number, the basis, and the decision. Say the last part only if it's true.
Base salary can't move
Move the mix, hold the total
I understand. Is there flexibility elsewhere? A sign-on bonus, more equity, or an earlier compensation review would get us to the same place.
A path to your total through parts that come out of a different budget. Check repayment terms before counting a sign-on bonus as cash.
You have another offer
Only what's true
I want to be upfront: I have another written offer, and I need to respond by [date]. This team is my first choice. If we can get to [$X], I'll sign this week.
Real leverage. In our experience, a competing offer is the most reliable way to move a number, so it's worth finishing other processes. Never invent one.
The deadline is too short
Ask for a date
I'm taking this seriously and want to give you a real answer. Could I get back to you by Friday? If that's a problem, can you tell me what's driving the timing?
A specific date, and a chance to learn whether the deadline is a real constraint.
The answer is no
Decide, don't drift
Thanks for checking. Let me think it over and get back to you by [day].
Time to decide whether the package works as it is. You don't owe anyone a second counter.
Close it in writing
After the call, send a short note that sums up where you landed. It keeps the recruiter's version and yours the same when they go for approval.
What you can send
Thanks for the time today. To recap: you're going to check on [the change] to get the total to [$X]. If that works, I'm ready to sign. Looking forward to hearing back.
Check that every agreed change is in the written offer before you sign.
List base and one-time payments separately from target or discretionary pay.
Read sign-on repayment terms and any conditions attached to the offer.
Confirm title, level, location, schedule, start date, and review timing.
Compare benefits by what they're worth to you, not by a headline total.
Once you sign, close the loop with any other companies kindly. You may want to work with them later.

Tech offer negotiation
Tech offers · a twelve-minute guide
Compare your tech offer year by year.
The base salary is usually straightforward. Bonuses and equity need a closer look: what will you receive, when, and under what conditions?
Ready to make a counteroffer?
Check the conditions behind each amount
A compensation total can combine base salary with bonuses and equity that depend on performance, vesting, or a future share price. Check how each part is earned and paid before comparing offers.
Year one
List the base paid during the year, sign-on payment and any repayment conditions, bonus under its actual rules, and equity scheduled to vest.
Later years
Check what remains after a sign-on ends, how vesting changes, and whether future grants or bonuses are documented or only customary.
Understand what your equity could be worth
Ask what the award is, what it costs to own, when it becomes yours, and whether you will be able to sell it. A grant can be valuable. It can also be worth nothing.
Restricted stock units (RSUs)
A promise to deliver shares

Confirm the number of units, the vesting schedule, what event delivers the shares, and what happens if you leave. At a public company, current share price can help model value, but future value is still unknown. At a private company, settlement and liquidity may depend on additional events.
Stock options
The right to buy shares

Ask for the option count, strike price, current common-share fair market value, vesting schedule, expiration date, post-termination exercise window, and liquidity restrictions. To estimate possible proceeds, compare the share value with the strike price and account for exercise costs, taxes, and whether you can sell the shares.
Questions to ask about your grant
Take these to the recruiter
What type of award is this, and how many units or options are included?
What vests in each year, and is there a cliff or other trigger?
For options, what are the strike price and latest common-share fair market value?
Will the company share a fully diluted share count or ownership percentage?
What is the exercise window after leaving, and can it change?
How have employees historically obtained liquidity? Is any future event guaranteed?
Check the tax consequences
Award and timing matter

Tax treatment differs across RSUs, incentive stock options, nonqualified stock options, location, timing, and individual circumstances. Use this guide to know what to ask, then confirm the consequences with a qualified tax professional before exercising or making an election.
Level affects more than your title
Your level can affect your responsibilities, promotion timing, future salary range, and equity. Check that it matches the job you discussed in interviews.
Ask for the formal level and the range attached to your work location.
Compare the responsibilities discussed in interviews with the written role.
Ask how performance is evaluated at that level and what the next level requires.
Treat external leveling data as a clue, not a company promise.

I want to make sure the level matches the scope we discussed. The role includes [specific responsibility]. How did the team map that scope to [offered level], and what would distinguish the next level?
The responsibilities you want the team to compare with its level expectations. Their answer can help you decide whether the offered role matches what you want.
Choose what to negotiate
Once you understand the package, choose the one or two changes that would matter most to you. Explain what you are asking for and why.
The year-one gap
Sign-on, base, or vesting
When I compare the offers year by year, this package is [X] lower in year one because [specific reason]. This role is my preference. Is there room to close that gap through [term]?
The actual comparison and the term you want reviewed.
Put salary, bonus, equity, and one-time pay on the same footing
before you quote a gap. Do not imply another offer exists unless it does.
The equity grant is hard to value
Ask before you counter
Before I compare the equity, could you share the grant type, vesting schedule, and the information the company provides candidates to understand strike price or current share value?
A request for missing facts. You are not assigning private equity a value the company has not supported.
The level does not match the scope
Make the mismatch visible

Several responsibilities we discussed, including [specific responsibility], appear closer to [level] scope. Could the team revisit the level, or clarify which responsibilities would change at the offered level?
The specific responsibility you want clarified. The team may explain the existing level, revisit it, or adjust the responsibilities.
Get the revised offer in writing.
After you agree on a change, check that the updated offer includes it before you sign.

How do I ask for a referral?
Most job help comes through acquaintances, but one close contact counts for more. Who to ask for a referral, and what to send, from two large network studies.
Ask widely, and lean on people who know your work. Across 6 million Facebook users, most job help came through acquaintances, because people have so many. One close tie was worth more.
From a peer-reviewed study of 6 million Facebook users (Gee, Jones & Burke, Journal of Labor Economics, 2017).
Social Networks and Labor Markets: How Strong Ties Relate to Job Finding on Facebook's Social Network
A causal test of the strength of weak ties
Who to ask

Two large studies of real networks agree on the shape. Most people get job help from someone they know less well, simply because they know so many more of them. But one close contact counts for more than one acquaintance.
So ask more than your closest friends, and put the most care into the people who’ve seen your work.
Start with people who've seen your work.
Former managers, teammates and clients can say what you did. In field experiments,
Then go one step out.

Someone you share a few connections with, like a former teammate’s new colleague, is the kind of tie that went with the most job moves in LinkedIn’s experiments. Ask the person you know well to introduce you.
Send everything in one message.
The job link, your resume, and two or three sentences they can paste into the referral form: how you know each other, and what you’d bring to this role.
Make no easy to say.
They’re putting their name next to yours. “No worries if it’s not a fit” keeps the relationship either way.
What a referral does on the recruiter’s side
Our take:

this is recruiter experience, not a finding from the studies below. Every application a recruiter opens shows whether someone referred you, and when a role has hundreds of applicants, that gets your resume read. It doesn’t make the decision for you. Once it’s open,
, the same as everyone else’s.
Is it ready for a real read?
The write-up in your report says what a recruiter takes from your resume first. Check it before someone vouches for you. The report can’t tell you who to ask; it reads the resume they’ll open.
The evidence
Whether anyone made a formal referral, or how they asked. Working alongside a friend is a stand-in for help, not a record of it.
Referrals specifically. It measures moving to a new job, on one platform, not who referred whom.
Neither study tested how to word a referral request. The four moves above are our advice.
Both studies use one platform’s data, so they describe its users, not every job seeker.

Software helps us sort. For roles with a big pile, an employer may set knockout questions that reject anyone who answers a certain way, or turn on a tool that ranks people by how well they match. When a role draws a thousand applicants, some of us just search the pile for the words the job needs.

A person still decides who moves forward. For a niche role, or one with fewer applicants, we usually read everyone. So write for the person: use the job’s own words where they’re true, answer the application questions carefully, and be wary of any tool that promises a score for what an ATS thinks of you.

Not with one magic score. The software pulls your text into fields, and if it can’t, someone enters the details by hand. Automatic rejection runs on application questions, not on your resume’s formatting.

From a file to a recruiter record

The parser reads the file, extracts information such as contact details and work history, and places it into structured fields. Employer rules, searches, filters, and human review happen after that and vary by system and company.

What can actually break

Greenhouse lists image-based resumes, graphics, word art, complex tables, headers, footers, text boxes, and columned layouts among formatting patterns that can produce unsuccessful or partial parsing. Lever notes that image files are not parseable and recommends checking whether the document text can be highlighted. Those layouts are what
sells, so export the PDF and check that its text can be selected.
A failed parse doesn't make the resume disappear. Greenhouse attaches the file to the candidate and asks the recruiter to enter the details by hand, and Lever describes the same fix.
Parsing is not the whole selection process

Once the details are stored, recruiters can filter applications by fields such as status, source, education, and answers to custom questions, and workflows differ by employer. Automatic rejection does exist, but in Greenhouse and Lever's documentation it runs on answers to application questions, often called knockout questions, not on resume formatting.
Both let employers reject or archive applicants automatically on an answer like “Do you have a commercial driver's license?” The parser itself is only the extraction step.
Where software does screen people out, it is mostly elsewhere:
which job ads you see, whether you’re eligible, and how you reach a person
. And once the file is in front of a person, the question is the reader, who isn’t immune to software either: in one experiment,
an algorithm’s recommendation swayed recruiters who said they trusted it less than a person

EEOC guidance on employment tests and selection procedures, issued in 2007 and not specific to software, says a screen that disproportionately excludes people by race, sex, or another protected trait has to be job-related and consistent with business necessity.
Practical takeaways
Use standard section headers so both parsers and humans can navigate quickly.
Write role titles and core skills in plain language, not internal jargon.
Avoid graphics or tables that disrupt parsing and readability.
A single column with clear headings, consistent dates, and standard section names is the safest baseline.
Use the role's language where it truthfully describes your experience. Don't stuff hidden or repeated keyword blocks into the file. A scanner's match rate is
the vendor's own model of an ATS, not the employer's

Your report is a recruiter's read of the page, not an ATS score. It works from the text we pull from your file, so it can't tell you how a particular employer's software or filters will treat it.

The Upturn report follows four stages of hiring: sourcing (including job ads), screening, interviewing, and selection. Once you have an opportunity to apply, check that your file contains readable text and clear sections. That addresses a possible parsing problem, not the broader risks documented in the report, and even then

Our advice:
make your relevant experience explicit, too. You can't fix bias in the tools, but you can keep an avoidable parsing problem from becoming another one.
What can you control?
Your report reads the resume you submit and flags what's missing or unclear. It can't see an employer's job ads or screening tools, and it doesn't guess at their settings.

How do I explain a career break?

Briefly, and only with what’s true. Naming caregiving did no better than silence in the UK, and worse than a layoff in the US. Keep the line plain and save the story for the interview.

What the experiment actually tested

In April 2020, 445 recruiters in Flanders, Belgium, rated Dutch-language resumes from recent graduates with zero, two, or five spelling errors, across eight occupations. Both error conditions lowered the hypothetical interview rating, with a larger penalty at five errors.

It justifies a careful spelling pass. It does not justify pretending one typo always ends the process, extending a Dutch-language result from Belgium to every language or labor market, or treating error-free writing as proof of job performance.

It also can't say whether spelling matters more than content: the study kept the content the same and changed only the spelling. In one study, accounting students had mock structured interviews before applying for real internships. Interviewers rated them during the first few minutes of small talk, before the formal questions began. Candidates who made a better first impression got higher final ratings from the same interviewer (a correlation of .42) and more real internship offers (.22). Those are moderate links, not destiny. The resume is usually what a recruiter reads first, and our experience is that it works the same way. The eye-tracking evidence points the same direction:

. Once a recruiter decides who you are, everything after that gets read through it.
A clear thread beats a scattered list

A study of a large freelance marketplace looked at how the order of someone's past jobs affected whether they were hired. Employers favored people who had moved in steps between related kinds of work over those whose history jumped around or never moved at all. The effect was stronger for complex jobs and less experienced workers, and weaker when the employer had already worked with the person. Someone who knows you doesn't need the resume to tell the story.

Those evaluations were written by an employer, not by the worker, so the lesson carries over to a resume only by analogy.

What changed, and what did not
Clearer writing helped employers recognize ability that was already there.
Algorithmic Writing Assistance on Jobseekers’ Resumes Increases Hires
What the experiment tested

In June and July 2021, a large online freelance marketplace randomly gave about half of its new jobseekers a writing tool inside the profile box. It underlined errors and suggested fixes for spelling, grammar, punctuation, and word choice. It wasn't generative: it couldn't be prompted, and it couldn't write anything for them.
The profile served as the resume, and it was short: about 70 words on average. More than 80% of the jobseekers were based outside the US, the UK, Canada, and Australia.
What the experiment found

In the control group, 3.1% of jobseekers were hired within their first 28 days. With the tool, 3.3% were. That's an 8% relative increase, with a 95% confidence interval of 3% to 13%. Treated jobseekers didn't send more applications, and the study found no evidence that employers were less satisfied with them, which argues against the idea that better writing merely disguised weaker candidates. The direction matches a recruiter experiment that varied only the spelling:
five spelling errors cost 1.85 points on a 0–10 interview rating

Of the 480,948 jobseekers randomized, the analysis covers the 194,700 whose profiles were submitted, approved by the platform, and not empty. The tool didn't change who submitted a profile or who was approved.

Our advice:
use wording that explains your actual experience. Start with the most useful detail,
what changed, how you measured it, and what you did to get there

The setting is narrow: one freelance platform, short profiles, mostly non-native English writers, and hires within 28 days. Treat the 8% as evidence that writing matters, not as a promise for a full resume in salaried hiring.

It can't tell you whether letting AI rewrite your resume helps: the tool only suggested corrections to what each person wrote.

What does the report cover?

What a recruiter is likely to take from your resume, what comes through clearly, and where they’d need more detail. Every card quotes the line it is about, says what a recruiter can’t tell from it, and gives an example with blanks only you can fill. Add a job posting, and the report reads your resume against that role too.
How is this different from ATS keyword tools?

Keyword tools count matches. The report reads for what you did and what changed because of it. It quotes the line behind every note and asks for the facts that are missing, instead of handing you a keyword score.
the software pulls your text into fields, and automatic rejection runs on application questions, not on a match score
Does a person read my resume?
No. A recruiter with 15 years in hiring wrote the review criteria, and AI applies them to your resume. Nobody reads individual reports, so check every suggested edit against what you actually did.
an algorithm’s recommendation swayed recruiters even when they said they trusted it less than a person
What file formats are supported?
PDF and Word documents (.docx), up to 4 MB. If we can’t read the file, paste the resume text instead. Formatting doesn’t matter; we only need the words.
What happens to uploaded resume data?

We don't store the raw resume or job description from an anonymous run. A completed anonymous report output can be recovered in the same browser for up to 24 hours, then expires automatically. Sign in to save it to history; saved reports and your account can be deleted at any time.
Is my data used to train public models?

No. We do not opt your data into model training, and OpenAI API data is not used to train OpenAI models by default. OpenAI may retain abuse-monitoring logs containing customer content for up to 30 days.

Delete individual reports from Reports. In Settings, you can export your account data or delete your account entirely.

You can keep opening your saved reports and downloading their PDFs; that comes with signing in, not with the pass. Another report requires a new pass or available free access.
